newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada auto union head hopes for deal with GM soon.
newsitem.headline: Canada auto union head hopes for deal with GM soon.

text.p: Canadian Auto Workers union President Buzz Hargrove said Monday he was hopeful an agreement could be reached with General Motors Corp. within a few hours to end a strike by 26,000 Canadian auto workers.
"We have some tough hurdles to jump," Hargrove told a televised news conference during an afternoon break in talks with GM chief negotiator Dean Munger.

"But we are both determined and our bargaining committees are determined that we're going to keep at this thing and hopefully sometime in the next ... two, three or four hours, we'll be able to announce a tentative agreement," he said.
The CAW said late Monday that Hargrove would brief reporters at 9 p.m. EDT 0100 GMT on progress towards a deal with GM.

The union and GM earlier expressed optimism that a tentative pact could be hammered out by an agreed deadline of noon EDT 1600 GMT to end the strike that paralysed GM plants in Canada and resulted in thousands of layoffs in the United States and Mexico.

"We're working like hell, in spite of the fact that we are dog tired, to try and bring a conclusion to this long and difficult dispute," Hargrove told reporters. "We certainly agree that we have come a long way, come far enough to put the extra effort in."

He said the union would allow General Motors to sell two of its Canadian parts plants. He said the Windsor, Ontario trim plant and the Oshawa, Ontario, fabrication plant, which employ a total of about 3,400 CAW members, would be put up for sale.
"Windsor trim will be sold," he said.
In answer to a question about the Oshawa fabrication plant, he replied, "The same."
Hargrove declined to provide further details.
GM spokesman Stew Low later confirmed that GM would sell the two plants, but he also told reporters that the workers involved would be covered by the new agreement with the CAW.
Talks between the CAW and GM aimed at ending a strike by 26,000 Canadian auto workers are stuck over the union's refusal to accept mandatory overtime at GM's Oshawa factory.
Low, echoing Hargrove, said he believed a deal could be reached in up to three hours. "Let's say about two or three hours," Low said in an interview.
The strike, which began at midnight Oct. 2, has also idled 18,371 assembly line and plant workers in the United States and Mexico, GM said Monday.

Negotiators said there was enough agreement on other crucial issues, such as outsourcing -- shifting work to outside, often non-union plants -- to give them some confidence that an overall pact could be reached in accordance with the labour agreement pattern that the union set at Chrysler Corp. last month.

Shifts have been cancelled at four car assembly plants in the United States -- in Orion Township, Mich; Fairfax, Kansas; Wentzville, Mo. and Lansing, Mich. More than 2,000 workers are also idle at GM's transmission plant in Warren, Mich. and more than 1,000 at other plants in the state.
GM's stock gained 75 cents to $53.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
